description: Dependency cooldown. Almost every published supply-chain attack is caught and yanked within hours to days, so the cheapest defence is simply not to be first: waiting puts the detection window in front of us instead of behind. Of the ten incidents surveyed in https://blog.yossarian.net/2025/11/21/We-should-all-be-using-dependency-cooldowns, eight had a window under a week and 14 days would have covered all but xz-utils.

This repo is a closer fit for that threat model than most. tj-actions on that list was a compromised GitHub Action that exfiltrated CI secrets, and actions/checkout and actions/setup-node run here in jobs holding FORGE_API_TOKEN. Pinning them by SHA fixes WHICH commit runs; only the cooldown addresses whether that commit has been looked at by anyone yet.

The cost is bounded, and deliberately does not extend to security fixes: Renovate raises those as soon as it detects them, bypassing this cooldown with no configuration needed. That bypass is only as good as the detection behind it, though — Renovate learns a version is vulnerable from GitHub's vulnerability alerts, so if those are ever switched off for this repo, the cooldown keeps applying to security fixes with nothing left to exempt them. Keep them on. npm audit --omit=dev --audit-level=high gates every PR besides, so an unfixed high advisory in a shipped dependency turns the whole queue red until it is resolved.

semanticCommits: enabled makes Renovate title its PRs as Conventional Commits (chore(deps): ..., fix(deps): ... for security bumps). That is required now that PR titles are linted (.github/workflows/pr-title-lint.yml) and drive the release-please changelog: without it, every bot merge would be a non-conforming subject that fails the title check and lands ungrouped in the changelog.

packageRules.description: Both copies of Mermaid ship in the bundle. Bump them in one PR so the corpus parses them as a pair, rather than leaving one major green while the other is untested.

@vitejs/plugin-react v6 peers on vite v8, so bumping either alone can't resolve a lockfile (peer conflict + artifact failure). Group them so both majors land in one PR with a single consistent lockfile.

mermaid-10 is an alias (npm:mermaid@^10.9.3) and it exists to BE the pinned major-10 line — a diagram pinned to 10 must keep rendering as 10. Grouping does not enforce this; only allowedVersions does. Crossing to 11 here would silently defeat the version dropdown.
Pinned exact and deployed with production credentials, so a bump should be a reviewed PR that runs the full gate — never a floating @latest resolved on the runner.

Two separate hazards on the 22.x line, so the cap sits below both. (1) The Forge CLI refuses to run on the 22.23.1 and 24.17.0 builds exactly — its engines range is >=20.18.1 <22.23.1 || >22.23.1 <24.17.0 || >24.17.0. (2) From 22.23.0 onward the security releases regressed a keep-alive socket path so the CLI (still on node-fetch@2) throws ERR_STREAM_PREMATURE_CLOSE mid-request against Atlassian, failing lint AND deploy — nodejs/node#63989, Atlassian FRGE-1750. Neither is caught on a PR: as PR #8 showed for the engines block, the corpus job never invokes the CLI, so nothing that runs on a PR can fail on a bad Node build — only the deploy would. Renovate cannot read the node-version comments in the workflow, so this cap is the only thing stopping it re-proposing 22.23.x (it would target 22.23.0, the newest allowed under the old range). Hold at 22.22.x until Node ships the #63989 fix, then raise the cap past it.

description: The 14-day cooldown above is aimed at a NAMED dependency arriving at a NEW version — that is where a supply-chain attack enters, and where waiting buys a detection window. Lock file maintenance is a different shape: it re-resolves ~45 transitives at once, all of them already inside ranges this repo has committed to. A per-package cooldown on that is a treadmill rather than a delay — every rebase pulls in something freshly published, the stability clock restarts, and the PR can never merge. PR #97 demonstrated it: open from 2026-07-27 with every substantive check green, blocked only by renovate/stability-days, still unmerged nine days later. This exemption is what lets a lockfile refresh land at all.

Do not expect this rule to clear the Dependabot backlog — that was the reason it was added, and the reason was wrong. Measured when #97 finally merged: npm audit went from 38 findings to 37. Deleting package-lock.json and resolving the same package.json from scratch reproduces 37 identically, so the lockfile was never stale; those are simply the versions npm picks today. The dev-scope alerts live in the ~821-entry nested tree at node_modules/@forge/cli/node_modules, which a lockfile refresh does not reach. Neither do npm overrides — tried on undici, shell-quote and websocket-driver, and npm declined to apply them into that subtree at all, never recording an overrides block. The only lever that moves those versions is @forge/cli's own version: 13.2.0 to 13.3.0 takes the audit from 37 to 32.

So treat this rule as dependency hygiene — it keeps the lockfile from drifting arbitrarily far from what package.json declares — and not as a security control. The npm audit --omit=dev --audit-level=high gate in ci.yml is what guards the shipped bundle, and it has been at 0 findings throughout. Direct dependency updates keep the full 14 days; only the lockfile refresh is exempt, and it still has to pass the corpus, audit, Dependency Review and CodeQL jobs like any other PR.
